# Stop pricing projects by effort — price the cost of waiting

Last year I quoted a client €18,000 for a data-migration project. They said yes in four minutes. I spent the next two weeks convinced I had underpriced it — until I learned their old licence renewal, which the migration made cancellable, cost €31,000 a quarter. My price wasn't competing with my effort. It was competing with their cost of delay.

That reframe — price against the cost of waiting, not the cost of working — changed how I scope every fixed-price engagement. Here is the exact process I now use.

## The three-question scoping call

Before I estimate anything, I ask three questions, in this order:

1. **"What happens if this doesn't get done this quarter?"** The answer tells you whether you're selling a painkiller or a vitamin. If the honest answer is "nothing much," fixed-price is the wrong model — bill hourly and keep the engagement small.
2. **"What have you already tried?"** Every previous failed attempt raises the value of a working solution and lowers the client's confidence in cheap alternatives. Two failed attempts by internal teams is worth roughly a 40% premium in my experience — not because the work is harder, but because certainty is what they're now buying.
3. **"Who signs this off, and what do they get judged on?"** If the signer's bonus depends on the outcome, negotiate with the outcome. If they're a proxy for a committee, your real risk is scope drift, and the price needs a change-control clause more than a premium.

The order matters. Ask about budget first and you anchor to their number. Ask about delay first and you anchor to their loss.

## The 3x floor

My rule for the number itself: the price must be at least three times what the project costs me to deliver, and no more than one third of the first-year value to the client. If those two bands don't overlap, I don't take the project at a fixed price — the overlap is where both sides can win. Most of my early underpricing came from calculating the first band and never asking about the second.

A worked example: the migration cost me about 60 hours. At my internal rate that's a €6,000 floor, so 3x gives €18,000. Their first-year saving was €124,000, so a third gives a €41,000 ceiling. I quoted the floor of a very wide band — which is why they said yes in four minutes. Today I would quote €28,000 and expect a short negotiation. The four-minute yes is not a win; it's a pricing diagnostic.

## Why effort-based pricing keeps you poor

Effort pricing has a hidden ratchet: as you get better, the same outcome takes fewer hours, so your income per project falls precisely because your skill rose. Value pricing inverts that — the faster you get, the higher your effective rate, and the speed itself becomes a selling point ("live before your renewal date") instead of a discount trigger.

The strongest objection I hear is that clients demand hour breakdowns. They mostly don't. Procurement departments do — and for them I attach a milestone schedule instead: three dated deliverables, each tied to a payment, none mentioning hours. In six years exactly one procurement team has refused it.

If you want the deeper theory, Jonathan Stark's *Hourly Billing Is Nuts* covers the economics, but the practice comes down to the two numbers above: their cost of waiting, and your 3x floor. Get those in every scoping call and the price writes itself.
